Naqasima-Sobey, Milika.summary: Naqasima-Sobey's research traces the link between land, freshwater, and reef health across the Pacific — work rooted in her own village on the Sigatoka River, where women harvest freshwater mussels (kai) that first drew her into fisheries science. Her early studies tracked coral reef sedimentation and water quality around Fiji's lagoons, while later work examined how communities across the region actually manage water resources. She now advocates for treating Indigenous knowledge as essential to water governance, warning that oral traditions about water management risk being lost unless they are properly documented.

Tabudravu, Jioji.summary: Dr Tabudravu is a chemist who searches Fiji’s reefs — and increasingly other Pacific ecosystems — for new molecules that could become tomorrow’s medicines, an area known as marine natural product biodiscovery. In practical terms, his team isolates compounds from Fijian sponges (for example Aplysinella rhax and Stylotella aurantium) and tests whether they can inhibit malaria parasites, sleeping-sickness parasites, or cancer cells; his lab has also built database-driven screening tools that help scientists quickly spot genuinely new chemistry rather than re-isolating molecules already known to science. A son of Wainunu in Bua, he continues to link his UK lab back to Fijian universities and students.

Waqa-Sakiti, Hilda.summary: Waqa-Sakiti is a Fijian entomologist who has spent years combing Fiji's forests to describe long-horned beetles found nowhere else on Earth, including documenting the giant Xixuthrus heros — one of the world's largest beetles and a cultural totem for a Namosi chiefly clan. Her taxonomic surveys and species-distribution models reveal which native forests and host trees matter most for conserving these often-endemic insects. That grounding in fieldwork has widened into broader environmental work, from tracking tree cover loss across Pacific island catchments to leading rapid biodiversity assessments and environmental impact studies ahead of development projects. She has since become one of the region's leading women in science, mentoring young Pacific researchers while leading conservation projects across the islands.

Waqalevu, Viliame.summary: Waqalevu works on one of aquaculture's hardest early bottlenecks: keeping baby fish alive and healthy in their first days of life. His research on feeding rotifers with enriched microalgae and oils has improved survival and growth in hatchery-raised Japanese flounder and red sea bream larvae, species central to Japan's seafood industry. He has also studied how the digestive systems and hormones of fish larvae develop day by day, and has extended his work into coral reef and mangrove research across the Pacific, Middle East, and French Polynesia. He now leads live-feed and marine-rescue research at Yas SeaWorld in Abu Dhabi.

Lako, Jimaima.summary: Lako studies the foods Fijians actually eat — from garden vegetables to reef fish — to understand both their nutritional value and the risks they can carry. Her lab work measured antioxidants and glycemic index in dozens of Pacific foods, generating some of the first regional data linking traditional diets to protection against diabetes and heart disease. She has also traced how the shift toward processed, imported food has driven rising obesity in Fiji, and has worked on practical food-safety problems like ciguatera fish poisoning, and on building better supply chains for Pacific products like tilapia, sea grapes, and virgin coconut oil.

Ginigini, Joape.summary: Ginigini searches Fiji's coral reefs and marine sediments for bacteria that could become the next generation of antibiotics. His work helped describe six new species of Salinispora, a genus of marine bacteria already known for producing anticancer and antibiotic compounds, and has explored how competition between reef bacteria alters their antibiotic activity. He now also works on more applied marine science, including tools to detect and manage invasive marine species in Fiji and international standards for environmental DNA monitoring.

Wilson, Donald.summary: Wilson is a public health physician whose research spans two very different threats to Pacific health systems: drug-resistant hospital infections and the rising burden of diabetes. He has helped uncover ongoing outbreaks of carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii in Fiji's major hospitals, tracing how the superbug spreads between wards and even across Pacific borders. His diabetes research looks at where care is falling short, from how patients themselves understand diabetes self-care to the often-overlooked link between blood sugar control and dental costs, an interest that traces back to his earlier occupational health research in Japan on diabetes and medical spending. Together, the work aims to strengthen how Fiji's health system detects and manages both infectious and chronic disease.

Waqa, Gade.summary: Dr Waqa leads the Pacific Research Centre for the Prevention of Obesity and Non-Communicable Diseases (C-POND) — a WHO Collaborating Centre. Her work asks a very practical question: given that around 80% of deaths in Fiji come from lifestyle diseases like diabetes, heart disease and hypertension, how do you get good scientific evidence into the hands of the ministers and civil servants who actually write food and health policy? Through projects such as TROPIC (Translational Research for Obesity Prevention in Communities) she has trained government "knowledge brokers", studied salt and sugar intake, and pushed for measures such as sugar taxes and healthier food environments in schools and communities across the Pacific region.

Veitayaki, Joeli.summary: Veitayaki has spent decades studying and building community-based fisheries management in Fiji, starting with his own home community on Gau Island, where he helped set up the Lomani Gau network linking all 16 villages around shared environmental management. He researches how traditional resource-management systems can work alongside modern conservation science, and has published widely on Pacific ocean governance and the law of the sea. He is now a strategic advisor for Blue Prosperity Fiji, a national program surveying reefs across the country and putting that data directly into the hands of the coastal communities who depend on them.

Vada, Sera.summary: Vada studies what actually makes a trip good for the traveler, beyond simple enjoyment — drawing on positive psychology to measure tourists' deeper wellbeing rather than just satisfaction scores. Her PhD examined the hedonic and eudaimonic effects of travel, work that has grown into a research program spanning repeat visitors to Fiji, seniors' travel experiences, and Chinese tourists viewed through a Confucian lens. As a proud Fijian who has worked in her country's tourism industry, she is also motivated by how tourism wellbeing research can benefit host communities, not just visitors, including her work on inclusive water and sanitation access in Pacific tourism destinations.

Vunibola, Suliasi.summary: Vunibola studies how Indigenous Fijian communities build successful businesses and development projects on customary land — challenging the common assumption that communal land ownership is an obstacle to economic progress. Using the Vanua Research Framework and talanoa methods, his case studies of itaukei enterprises show how practices like solesolevaki (unpaid communal work) can be assets for locally driven, culturally grounded development rather than barriers to it. He has also written on how poorly designed foreign aid can create maladaptation rather than resilience in Pacific communities. His current work extends this thinking to Pacific-wide climate resilience research spanning Fiji, Vietnam, and the Philippines.

Vave, Ron.summary: Vave studies a striking Fijian practice that Western conservation science rarely examines: how the 100-night fishing ban that follows a chief's funeral doubles as an accidental marine protected area. His doctoral research on Indigenous Fijian funerals asked how this tradition shapes both social bonds and reef health, and whether it still holds as urbanization changes Fijian communities. Drawing on 14 years as a Locally Managed Marine Area practitioner across the Indo-Pacific, he now researches how cultural practices and ecosystem services are deeply intertwined, comparing Indigenous fishing and resource governance across Fiji, Hawai'i, and Papua New Guinea.

Tuiwawa, Marika.summary: Tuiwawa is a field entomologist and biodiversity researcher who has helped document Fiji's insect life, including describing a new species of forest damselfly on Vanua Levu. His broader fieldwork spans rapid biodiversity assessments of forests and mangroves across Fiji, contributions to the East Melanesian Islands Biodiversity Hotspot profile, and Fiji's national inventory of invasive alien species.

Tarai, Jope.summary: Tarai studies how Fijians actually use social media to organize, campaign, and cope with crisis — from elections to cyclones. His research on Fiji's 2014 and 2018 elections traced how political parties adapted their social media tactics over time, while a separate study of Tropical Cyclone Winston showed how hashtags like #StrongerThanWinston helped Fijians share information and build solidarity during the country's worst storm in decades. He has also examined how Christian communities interpreted Cyclone Winston as divine judgment, and writes more broadly on internet censorship, digital feminism, and decolonizing foreign aid in the Pacific.

Rokolekutu, Ponipate.summary: Rokolekutu examines why most iTaukei landowners remain economically marginalized in Fiji despite owning nearly 90% of the country's land. His research traces this paradox to colonial-era institutions like the iTaukei Land Trust Board, arguing that the very structures built to protect Indigenous land rights also entrenched Indigenous economic dependency. He has also challenged the standard narrative that Britain's annexation of Fiji was an act of benevolence, showing it was instead driven by imperial economic interests. His teaching and writing connect this land history to present-day struggles for Indigenous sovereignty across Oceania.

Ravuvu, Amerita.summary: Ravuvu works on the politics behind the Pacific's fight against non-communicable diseases — the diabetes, obesity, and heart disease that now cause most deaths in the region. Her research into sugar-sweetened beverage taxes in Fiji and Vanuatu traces how industry lobbying and trade pressures can water down policies designed to curb sugar consumption, even when the health case is clear. She has also examined the political economy behind Fiji's sugar tax as a rare health-and-economic 'win-win', and written on scaling up food pricing policy and empowering youth across the region to push for stronger NCD prevention.

Tawake, Alifereti.summary: Tawake pioneered a community-led approach to reviving Fiji's coastal fisheries that has since spread to twenty countries worldwide. It began in the 1990s in Verata, a small mudflat community whose clam population had collapsed; working with villagers, he helped clam numbers rebound 24-fold by reviving traditional no-take periods, work that won him a Whitley Award for conservation. That local success grew into the Fiji Locally-Managed Marine Area Network, now covering over a quarter of Fiji's inshore waters and formally adopted by the Fiji government. His more recent research looks at what makes these community-led networks endure, including the often-overlooked role women play in governing coastal fisheries.

Ravulo, Jioji.summary: Prof. Ravulo’s work is grounded in social work with Pacific young people in Australia — how they navigate marginalisation, mental health and drug and alcohol issues, and what it takes for them to feel they belong. Drawing on his own upbringing in Western Sydney public housing, he built PATHE, a Pacific student support program now running in more than 80 New South Wales schools, and led early research on refugee youth attitudes to alcohol and other drugs. He describes his practice as moving beyond the individual to the collective — helping people feel cared for, connected, and that they matter.

Ratuva, Steven.summary: Ratuva is a political sociologist who studies how Pacific societies respond to upheaval — from military coups and pandemics to climate change — and how indigenous knowledge can inform policy. He led the Pacific Ocean and Climate Crisis Assessment project, a 16-country study pairing Indigenous knowledge systems with climate science. His work on social protection during the pandemic examined how Pacific communities drew on solidarity and traditional support networks to weather Covid-19. In 2023 he became the first Pacific Islander appointed Pro-Vice-Chancellor Pacific, capping decades of research on coups, ethnicity, and regional security.

His fieldwork, often conducted alongside researchers at USP's Institute of Applied Sciences, has also documented the less visible cultural and psychological losses and damages that climate change causes in Fijian communities, beyond the physical and financial costs typically measured.

This fieldwork builds the ecological baseline data used for conservation and land-use planning in these remote highland areas.

Nakoro, Elia.summary: Nakoro is an archaeologist whose fieldwork has documented Fiji's deep human history, from Lapita pottery that reveals 3,000-year-old trade and settlement patterns to fortified hilltop sites in Bua Province. He has also researched the geography and oral history behind vanished islands like Vuniivilevu and Burotu, and works alongside biologists on rapid cultural and environmental surveys of Fiji's forests and river systems.

Naivalu, Kelera.summary: Naivalu's research digs into a basic but under-studied question for rural Fiji: whether the pit latrines and septic systems people actually use are safe, and whether the water coming out of village taps is too. Her fieldwork across 29 rural communities found E. coli contamination linked to poorly designed latrines, while a companion study on household perceptions of drinking water found many villagers misjudge how clean their water really is. As part of the Watershed Interventions for Systems Health project, she works with communities and water committees to fix these problems across the whole watershed rather than one tap or toilet at a time.

Nainoca, Winifereti.summary: Nainoca's doctoral research asked why some Fijian villages succeed at protecting their reefs and lagoons while others struggle, and found the answer in bula vakavanua — the traditional Fijian way of life. Her study of three coastal communities showed that kinship ties, traditional ecological knowledge, and talanoa (dialogue as storytelling) sustain community-based marine conservation more than external rules or funding ever could. She has since broadened this community-first lens to examine how global development goals can be adapted to fit local, place-based understandings of wellbeing in the Pacific.

Nabobo-Baba, Unaisi.summary: Nabobo-Baba created the Fijian Vanua Research Framework, a now widely used method that asks researchers working with iTaukei communities to follow Fijian cultural protocol — seeking permission from the vanua, using talanoa, and giving back to the community — rather than importing Western research norms wholesale. Her own doctoral study of her home district of Vugalei explored how Indigenous Fijians actually acquire and pass on knowledge, with findings that reshaped how she thinks education, curriculum, and even school design should work in Fiji. She has since applied this same decolonizing lens to topics as varied as the history of Fijian higher education and climate change's health impacts in the Pacific.

His studies with the Wildlife Conservation Society and Conservation International documented how much food and income Fijian women bring home from fishing, work that had previously gone uncounted in national fisheries data. He has also compared different methods for monitoring reef fish, tracked hawksbill turtle nesting sites, and worked on water, sanitation, and hygiene programs in Melanesia's informal settlements — applying the same close, community-based fieldwork across very different conservation and development challenges.

Meo-Sewabu, Litea.summary: Meo-Sewabu studies how Indigenous Fijian communities understand health, wellbeing, and vulnerability — and how research itself should be conducted ethically within those communities. Her doctoral work developed the Tanoa Health Belief Framework, a lens for understanding wellbeing among Marama iTaukei (Indigenous Fijian women) built on an Indigenous research method she calls 'Tali Magimagi'. She has since applied that same community-first approach to practical problems, from co-designing Australia's kava importation policy with Pacific communities to studies on violence against children and gender-inclusive sanitation in informal settlements. Her recent work on Talanoa-based mental health research continues that effort to build culturally safe support for Pacific communities in Australia.

His concept of 'peripherality' — how far a community sits from services and roads — has helped explain why some Fijian villages cope with disasters and climate change better than others, based on fieldwork along the 200-km cross-island road on Viti Levu. He has also studied the emotional and cultural toll of planned village relocations, and argues that relocation policy too often overlooks tradition and local knowledge in favor of purely technical solutions.

Finau, Glenn.summary: Finau is an accounting scholar who studies how systems built to measure money and value often clash with Indigenous ways of relating to land and resources. His research on customary land and 'land banking' in Fiji shows how accounting techniques can quietly dispossess communities of communally owned land. He has also examined how Fijians drew on religious belief to make sense of Cyclone Winston, and how social media has helped diaspora communities like Rotumans sustain cultural identity online. As a Pacific Ocean Accounts Fellow, he now works on building accounting frameworks that help Pacific nations value and manage their ocean resources.

Aporosa, Apo.summary: Aporosa studies kava — the culturally significant Pacific drink — not as a novelty substance but as it's actually used in traditional settings, where it plays a central role in Pacific social life and identity. His research challenges studies that test kava in tablet form, showing that traditionally consumed kava affects cognition very differently than lab-based extracts, with real implications for road-safety rules that don't distinguish between the two. He is now leading a clinical trial testing traditional kava circles as therapy for PTSD, drawing on the same cultural spaces he has studied for two decades. His broader work on diasporic kava use and identity argues that Pacific health research needs its own culturally grounded methods, not borrowed Western frameworks.
